```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(flexdashboard)
library(plotly)
library(rjson)
library(wesanderson)
source("compmus.R")

  
```


### Chroma-based Self-similarity matrix

```{r}
"features/elze-s-2.json" |>                           # Change the track
  compmus_chroma(norm = "identity") |>                 # Change the norm
  compmus_self_similarity(
    feature = pc,
    distance = "euclidean"                             # Change the distance
  ) |>   
  ggplot(aes(x = xtime, y = ytime, fill = d)) + 
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(guide = "none") +               # Change the colours?
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_classic()+
  ggtitle("Chroma-based self-similarity matrix of 'Random Fish's Name'\n by Common Sexuality")+theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))# Change the theme?

```


------------------------------------------------------------------------

On the left you can see the chroma-based self-similarity matrix of my band's song "Random Fish's Name".As is indicated in this matrix, the song is homogeneous in terms of harmony, as it is based on a few chords which are playing repetitively. The 'small' blue squares in the beginning, middle and end of the song indicate the usage of ambient sounds and sound effects.


### Timbre based self-similarity matrix

```{r}
"features/elze-s-2.json" |>                           # Change the track
  compmus_mfccs(norm = "identity") |>                  # Change the norm
  compmus_self_similarity(
    feature = mfcc,
    distance = "euclidean"                             # Change the distance
  ) |>   
  ggplot(aes(x = xtime, y = ytime, fill = d)) + 
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(guide = "none") +               # Change the colours?
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_classic()+
  ggtitle("Timbre-based self-similarity matrix of 'Random Fish's Name'\n by Common Sexuality")+theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))     

```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

On the left you can see the timbre based self-similarity matrix of my band's song "Random Fish's Name". The song begins with sounds of crackling fireplace and water drops, which is constituted by the 'small navy square' in the left bottom corner. As the guitar joins in in the 20th second of the song, followed by vocals and ambient noises, the timbre becomes more varied. This variation is increased even more when bass and drums comes in, expanding the sphere of timbre even more with added low frequencies. The two 'big navy squares' in the top right show the timbre similarity of two verses and two choruses. The instruments (2 guitars, drums, bass and vocals) in all of them are not only the same but also perform almost identical parts, which is what makes those squares appear. The small gap between those squares indicates a guitar solo, which disrupts the timbre similarity.


### Chromagram

```{r}
"features/elze-s-2.json" |>                           # Change the track
  compmus_chroma(norm = "identity") |>                 # Change the norm
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = pc, fill = value)) + 
  geom_raster() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = 0:11,
    minor_breaks = NULL,
    labels = c(
                "C", "C#|Db", "D", "D#|Eb",
                "E", "F", "F#|Gb", "G",
                "G#|Ab", "A", "A#|Bb", "B"
              )
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(guide = "none") +               # Change the colours?
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_classic()+
  ggtitle("Chromagram of 'Random Fish's Name' by Common Sexuality")+theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

```

### Cepstogram

```{r}
"features/elze-s-2.json" |>                           # Change the track
  compmus_mfccs(norm = "identity") |>                  # Change the norm
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = mfcc, fill = value)) + 
  geom_raster() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = 0:12,

```

### What contributes to the valence of the song?

![Photo by Kate Kunz/Corbis](https://i.dailymail.co.uk/i/pix/2013/05/15/article-2325004-19CBB2DF000005DC-701_1024x615_large.jpg)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

One might suppose that songs that are faster, more upbeat are 'happier' than slow ones because of how 'happiness' is defined stereotipically. However, that's not the case, at least in AI music world. In the next tab you can see a scatter plot which denies this presupposition.

### Arousal is key to valence

```{r}
aisc2024<- read_csv("aisc2024.csv")
aisc2024 |>                   # Start with the data
  ggplot(                     # Set up the plot.
    aes(
      x = tempo,
      y = arousal,
      colour = valence
    )
  ) +
  geom_point() +              # Scatter plot.
  
  
  scale_x_continuous(         # Fine-tune the x axis.
    
    minor_breaks = NULL       # Remove 'minor' grid lines.
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(         # Fine-tune the y axis in the same way.
    
    minor_breaks = NULL
  ) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +  # Use the popular viridis colour palette.
  scale_size_continuous(      # Fine-tune the sizes of each point.
    trans = "exp",            # Use an exp transformation to emphasise loud..
    guide = "none"            # Remove the legend for size.
  ) +
  theme_light() +             # Use a simpler theme.
  labs(                       # Make the titles nice.
    x = "Tempo",
    y = "Arousal",
    colour = "Valence"
  )+
  ggtitle("Relationship between tempo, arousal and valence/n in 2024 AI Song Contest")+theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
ggplotly()
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

On left you can see a scatter plot, which indicates the relationship between arousal, tempo and valence features in 2024 AI Song Contest's applications. At the bottom right corner one can see that songs, that are fast but don't evoke much arousal, score lower in valence than the songs with slow tempo but higher arousal. The minimum amount of arousal for obvious effect on valence seems to be 4.25. Arousal is probably not the only contributor to the valence of the song. Further research is needed to summarize what creates valence. Maybe it's the liveliness or the loudness of the track that makes it seem 'happier'?
